Long Description / Review Note:
This figure explains that a LAION-5B image-text sample should be understood as a governable candidate record rather than a simple pair of one
  image and one caption. The center of the diagram is a stable candidate record with fields such as uid, image_url, text, clip_score, nsfw_score,

  threshold, while emphasizing that CLIP score only measures image-text relevance and is not full quality assurance. The risk channel records NSFW,
  watermark, face-privacy, and license-hint signals. The release channel records dataset version, shard identifier, and removal status. On the

Chapter / Contribution Title: Chapter 39: Image-Text Data Engineering: Candidate Pool Construction, Multimodal Filtering, and DataComp Evaluation
Caption / Figure Title: Figure 39-2 Image-text candidate-pool quality evaluation and closed-loop repair
Markdown Alt: Figure 39-2 Image-text candidate-pool quality evaluation and closed-loop repair
Alt Text for Submission: Image-text candidate-pool quality evaluation and closed-loop repair. Source: original illustration based on the LAION-5B paper and DataComp benchmark design.
Long Description / Review Note:
This figure describes a closed-loop quality evaluation and repair workflow for an image-text candidate pool. The process starts with candidate
  metadata, including URL, text, and quality scores. It then applies five-channel quality checks: the text channel checks caption noise and
  language confidence; the visual channel checks download success, image size, and image hash; the alignment channel checks CLIP score and human
  pass rate; the risk channel checks NSFW content, watermark, face privacy, and related safety risks; and the release channel checks manifest
  coverage, URL status, and the removal ledger.

  Samples that fail or raise uncertainty are routed into a risk queue. The queue includes URL decay, caption noise, watermark or copyright issues,
  NSFW content and minors, faces and privacy, and possible evaluation contamination. Repair actions include redownloading, refiltering,
  downweighting, quarantining, or removing problematic samples. After repair, approved data is written into a frozen training view, including the
  manifest, shards, and sample seed, so that experiments can be reproduced.

  The final stage evaluates candidate-pool filters under a fixed DataComp-style protocol: the model, hyperparameters, and benchmarks remain fixed,
  and only the data filtering strategy g changes. The formula S(g) represents a weighted benchmark score used to compare different filtering
  strategies. The main message is that image-text data quality should not rely on post-training fallback; quality should be controlled through
  channel checks, risk handling, repair actions, and reproducible evaluation before training.

Long Description / Review Note: The diagram presents the four-stage construction pipeline for SparseTable-Bench. Stage one collects table images from scientific papers, financial reports, and clinical-trial documents. The collection includes borderless tables, whitespace-based layouts, empty columns, and complex headers, while preserving source and dataset-split information. Stage two extracts a parseable HTML tree, preserves merged-row and merged-column relationships, and explicitly represents empty cells. Stage three assigns a spatial boundary to every cell, including blank cells, and checks row alignment, column alignment, and boundary validity. Stage four creates sparse-topology stress samples through column-aware masking. Text may be removed, but the row and column structure must remain intact. Consistency checks throughout the pipeline ensure that the HTML is parseable, cell order is preserved, spatial boundaries are valid, and dataset versions and splits remain aligned.

Long Description / Review Note: The diagram shows the STB-Mask-Stress sample-generation and evaluation workflow. First, the original table is parsed to obtain its HTML grid, rows, columns, and cell boundaries. Second, one or two candidate columns are selected randomly. Third, one of three masking modes is chosen: body masking, header masking, or random sparse masking. Fourth, the corresponding image regions are covered with a uniform background. Fifth, the annotations are updated by removing or resetting the masked text while preserving the table structure. Sixth, the generated samples are evaluated for structural similarity, empty-position recall, and different categories of error. Body masking preserves the header while hiding body columns. Header masking hides the header while preserving the body. Random sparse masking hides selected body cells to simulate scanning damage, occlusion, or local sparsity. Alt Text for Submission: Multi-turn structure of a tool-call trajectory. Tool observations return as new image inputs; the model must continue reasoning from the observation image rather than merely produce a formally correct call.
Long Description / Review Note:
This figure explains the structure of a multi-turn tool-call trajectory for medical image question
  answering. The sequence has four main steps connected from left to right. First, the task input comes from the user message and
  includes the original medical image, the question with candidate answer options, and metadata such as image index, image size,
  and region cues. Second, the assistant makes a decision action: it judges whether the whole-image evidence is sufficient,
  chooses whether to zoom in, run segmentation, or answer directly, and emits a valid tool name with JSON arguments when a tool
  is needed. Third, the tool or user message returns an observation, such as a crop, mask overlay, or segmentation result. This
  returned observation is inserted into the next dialogue turn while preserving the source region and tool arguments. Fourth, the
  assistant consumes the new observation, updates its judgment, calls tools again only if evidence is still insufficient, and
  finally outputs the selected option with a brief reason. A loop arrow shows that insufficient evidence sends the process back
  to the decision step. The core constraint is that tool-returned observations become part of the next context turn and remain
  traceable to the final answer.

Source reasoning traces from Dolci-Think-SFT-32B are first extracted and normalized. A teacher model then distills each long reasoning trace into two complementary components: a high-level solution intuition and a compressed explicit chain-of-thought. This diagram shows how text-to-video training data is processed from video sources into a trainable dataset. Public videos, CC0 asset libraries, and self-collected data are first segmented into single-shot clips, then filtered through motion detection to remove blurred, jittery, watermarked, or low-quality samples. The data is then stratified by resolution, quality tier, and SFT requirements, forming a trainable T2V dataset with manifests and audit logs.

This diagram shows a layered governance workflow for generative visual data, from safety blocking to quality routing. Data is first screened for hard-blocking risks such as adult content, CSAM, PII, and illegal samples, then reviewed for copyright risk, license status, opt-out lists, logos, watermarks, and brand marks.
